analysis.one_liner: Lets people sue government officials, including police, who violate their constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: Backed by 66 House members after the George Floyd protests, the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end 'qualified immunity,' a court-made rule that shields government employees from being personally sued when they violate someone's constitutional rights, unless the victim can point to a past court case with nearly identical facts. The bill would restore the 1871 civil rights law to what its supporters say it originally meant: an official who violates your rights can be held personally liable even if they believed they were acting lawfully. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and stayed there.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by state and local officials — including victims of police misconduct, excessive force, and unlawful searches. Under current law, many of these cases are thrown out before a jury ever hears them because no earlier case established the exact right in exactly the same situation. The bill would let a jury decide the violation itself.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the qualified immunity defense from lawsuits under 42 U.S.C. 1983, so that a defendant cannot escape liability by arguing they acted in good faith or that the right was not 'clearly established' at the time [S2][S3].

The bill's findings state that the 1871 Ku Klux Klan Act, now codified at section 1983, never included a good-faith defense, and that the Supreme Court created the doctrine in 1967 and expanded it in 1982, frustrating the law's original purpose [S3].
The bill states that the doctrine has 'severely limited the ability of many plaintiffs to recover damages' when their rights are violated by state and local officials [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Government employees, especially police officers, who would face personal liability in lawsuits; and ultimately taxpayers and municipalities, through damage awards, settlements, and higher liability insurance premiums.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves no protection for officials who make honest mistakes, exposing individual officers and other government workers to personal financial liability even when they reasonably believed their conduct was lawful [S2].

The costs of lawsuits would not fall only on individual officials — cities would face larger judgments and settlements, and those costs are ultimately paid by taxpayers, often through higher liability insurance premiums [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For someone whose rights have been violated, the change is the difference between getting compensation and getting nothing, since courts currently dismiss many valid claims on immunity grounds. The cost is real: honest officials could be sued for judgment calls, and local governments would pay more in judgments and insurance. Supporters of the bill argue those costs are what the 1871 law always intended, and that the threat of liability is what makes rights enforceable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee after its referral, never received a hearing, markup, or vote of any kind, and died when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 4, 2020, in the weeks after George Floyd's death, and was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S1][S5].
It drew 66 cosponsors — 65 House Democrats and 1 House Republican — alongside its Libertarian sponsor [S4].
The complete action history shows no committee action after the referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Government officials and police officers, who keep the qualified immunity defense that shields them from personal liability for constitutional violations, along with the municipalities and insurers that would otherwise bear the costs of judgments. Government officials who keep immunity from lawsuits.

for.name: Justin Amash
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ending Qualified Immunity Act and recruited the cosponsor list.

for.name: Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Joined Amash at introduction as the bill's lead Democratic cosponsor and helped recruit support.

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup for the bill after its referral to his committee; the record shows no committee action for the life of the bill.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; the House's police-reform vehicle that summer was a different bill that did not end qualified immunity.

against.name: Law enforcement groups and police unions
against.what_they_did: Opposed ending qualified immunity during the 2020 policing debate, arguing officers need the protection to do their jobs.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines but was thin: 65 of 231 House Democrats and 1 of 197 House Republicans signed on with the Libertarian sponsor, and the Democratic chairs who controlled the agenda never moved it.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: The bill removes the personal liability shield that protects officers from being sued for constitutional violations. Unions argued the shield is necessary; civil-rights plaintiffs say it is what keeps them from being compensated.

industries.industry: Municipal governments and their liability insurers
industries.note: Cities would face more judgments and settlements against their employees and higher liability insurance costs, costs passed to local taxpayers. Insurers and city budgets would bear the financial exposure.
